summary: Explains how to connect IPv6 islands over an IPv4 MPLS core using IPv6 Provider Edge routers. Dual-stack edge routers exchange IPv6 reachability with BGP, so the core only has to run IPv4 MPLS.

plainLanguage.summary: An MPLS core that runs IPv4 only can still carry IPv6 traffic if the edge routers speak both protocols. This RFC describes the 6PE approach: dual-stack routers at the edge of the core exchange IPv6 routes with BGP over IPv4, and forward IPv6 packets across the core using the same MPLS label-switched paths that IPv4 uses. No tunnels have to be configured by hand.

questions: how does ipv6 work over an ipv4 mpls core
what bgp next hop does 6pe use
how does ipv6 travel over an ipv4 mpls core
subtitle: Carrying IPv6 traffic across an IPv4 MPLS core by upgrading only the edge routers.

tldr.problem: A service provider with an IPv4 MPLS core usually wants to offer IPv6 to some customers without upgrading the core or hand-configuring tunnels.
tldr.mechanism: The 6PE approach makes the provider edge routers dual stack and has them exchange IPv6 prefixes with Multiprotocol BGP over IPv4, advertising their IPv4 address as an IPv4-mapped IPv6 next hop. The ingress edge router then labels the IPv6 packet directly and forwards it over the IPv4-signalled label-switched path.
tldr.outcome: The core keeps running IPv4 only, no tunnels need configuring, and no IPv4 header is put in front of the customer's IPv6 packets. The RFC also spells out the MTU that the MPLS links need, three ways to cross autonomous system boundaries, and the label spoofing risk that comes with exchanging labelled routes between operators.

facts.label: Labels imposed
facts.value: Two: an outer IPv4-signalled LSP label and an inner label bound to the IPv6 prefix

today: RFC 4798 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2007, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the specification of the 6PE approach for interconnecting IPv6 islands over an IPv4 MPLS core.

sections.title: Why the Edge Only
sections.content:
There are several approaches for providing IPv6 connectivity over an MPLS core network: requiring that MPLS networks support setting up IPv6-signalled Label Switched Paths and establishing IPv6 connectivity by using those LSPs, using configured tunnelling over IPv4-signalled LSPs, or using the IPv6 Provider Edge approach defined in this document.

The 6PE approach is required as an alternative to the use of standard tunnels. It provides a solution for an MPLS environment where all tunnels are established dynamically, thereby addressing environments where the effort to configure and maintain explicitly configured tunnels is not acceptable.

The approach requires that the edge routers connected to IPv6 islands be Dual Stack Multiprotocol-BGP-speaking routers, while the core routers are only required to run IPv4 MPLS. It uses MP-BGP over IPv4, relies on identification of the 6PE routers by their IPv4 address, and uses IPv4-signalled MPLS LSPs that do not require any explicit tunnel configuration.

An IPv6 island is a network running native IPv6, and a typical example is a customer's IPv6 site connected through its IPv6 Customer Edge router to one or more Dual Stack Provider Edge routers of a service provider. These 6PE routers are connected to an IPv4 MPLS core network.

The method typically applies to a provider that has an IPv4 MPLS network, is familiar with BGP, and wants to offer IPv6 to some of its customers without upgrading its core to IPv6. The provider only has to upgrade some provider edge routers so that they behave as 6PE routers, while leaving the IPv4 MPLS core untouched. No tunnels need to be explicitly configured, and no IPv4 headers need to be inserted in front of the IPv6 packets between the customer and the provider edge. The provider obtains IPv6 connectivity to its peers and upstreams by means outside the scope of the document, and its 6PE routers readvertise that connectivity over the IPv4 MPLS core with MP-BGP.

The 6PE approach provides global IPv6 reachability. Support of IPv6 VPNs is not within the scope of the document. Configuration and operations have a lot in common with an IPv4 or IPv6 VPN service over an IPv4 MPLS core, because all of them use MP-BGP to distribute non-IPv4 reachability information for transport over an IPv4 core, but the 6PE approach is somewhat simpler since it does not involve VPN concepts such as Virtual Routing and Forwarding tables.
sections.plainLanguage: There are several ways to give IPv6 connectivity over an MPLS core: requiring the network to set up IPv6-signalled label-switched paths, using configured tunnels over IPv4-signalled paths, or the 6PE approach in this RFC. 6PE is needed as an alternative to standard tunnels because it works where all tunnels are set up dynamically, so that configuring and maintaining explicit tunnels is not acceptable. The edge routers connected to IPv6 islands must be dual-stack routers that speak Multiprotocol BGP, while the core routers only have to run IPv4 MPLS. The provider upgrades some edge routers and leaves the core untouched, and no IPv4 header is inserted in front of the customer's IPv6 packets.

sections.title: The 6PE Routers
sections.content:
Each IPv6 site is connected to at least one Provider Edge router located on the border of the IPv4 MPLS cloud, and such a router is called a 6PE router. The 6PE router MUST be dual stack IPv4 and IPv6, and it MUST be configured with at least one IPv4 address on the IPv4 side and at least one IPv6 address on the IPv6 side. The configured IPv4 address needs to be routable in the IPv4 cloud, and there needs to be a label bound, via an IPv4 label distribution protocol, to this IPv4 route.

As a result, every 6PE router knows which MPLS label to use to send packets to any other 6PE router. An MPLS network offering BGP/MPLS IP VPN services already fulfills these requirements. No extra routes need to be injected in the IPv4 cloud.

The 6PE router receiving IPv6 packets from an IPv6 site is the ingress 6PE router, relative to those packets, and a 6PE router forwarding IPv6 packets to an IPv6 site is the egress 6PE router. The interface between the edge router of the IPv6 island and the 6PE router is a native IPv6 interface, which can be physical or logical. A routing protocol, an IGP or an EGP, may run between them for the distribution of IPv6 reachability information; alternatively, static routes or a default route may be used on the 6PE router and the CE router to control reachability. An IPv6 island may connect to the provider network over more than one interface.
sections.plainLanguage: An IPv6 island is a network running native IPv6, usually a customer site reached through the customer's own edge router. Each island connects to at least one provider edge router on the border of the IPv4 MPLS cloud, and that router is called a 6PE router. Every 6PE router must be dual stack, must have at least one IPv4 address on the IPv4 side and one IPv6 address on the IPv6 side, and its IPv4 address must be routable in the cloud with a label bound to it by a label distribution protocol. That is enough for every 6PE router to know which label to use to reach any other one, and no extra routes need to be injected into the IPv4 cloud.

sections.title: The Two Steps of the Exchange
sections.content:
Interconnecting IPv6 islands over an IPv4 MPLS cloud takes place through two steps.

First, the 6PE routers exchange IPv6 reachability information among themselves with MP-BGP. They MUST exchange the IPv6 prefixes over MP-BGP sessions running over IPv4, and the MP-BGP Address Family Identifier used MUST be IPv6, value 2. In doing so the 6PE routers convey their IPv4 address as the BGP Next Hop for the advertised IPv6 prefixes, and the IPv4 address of the egress 6PE router MUST be encoded as an IPv4-mapped IPv6 address in the BGP Next Hop field. This encoding is consistent with the definition of an IPv4-mapped IPv6 address as an address type used to represent the address of IPv4 nodes as IPv6 addresses. In addition, the 6PE MUST bind a label to the IPv6 prefix, and the Subsequence Address Family Identifier used in MP-BGP MUST be the label SAFI, value 4.

Second, the IPv6 packets are transported from the ingress 6PE router to the egress 6PE router over IPv4-signalled LSPs. The ingress 6PE router MUST forward IPv6 data over the IPv4-signalled LSP towards the egress 6PE router identified by the IPv4 address advertised in the IPv4-mapped IPv6 address of the BGP Next Hop for the corresponding IPv6 prefix.

As required by the BGP specification, provider edge routers form a full peering mesh unless route reflectors are used.
sections.plainLanguage: Interconnecting the islands takes two steps. First the 6PE routers exchange IPv6 prefixes over Multiprotocol BGP sessions that run over IPv4, using the IPv6 address family and the label sub-address family. In doing so they advertise their own IPv4 address as the next hop for the IPv6 prefixes, written as an IPv4-mapped IPv6 address. Second, the ingress 6PE router forwards the IPv6 data over the IPv4-signalled path towards the egress 6PE router named by that next hop address. The label-switched paths can be set up with any technique, but every implementation must support paths set up by LDP so that systems interoperate.

sections.title: Why Two Labels
sections.content:
When tunnelling IPv6 packets over the IPv4 MPLS backbone, rather than successively prepending an IPv4 header and then performing label imposition based on the IPv4 header, the ingress 6PE router MUST directly perform label imposition of the IPv6 header without prepending any IPv4 header. The outer label imposed MUST correspond to the IPv4-signalled LSP starting on the ingress router and ending on the egress router.

While the approach could theoretically operate in some situations using a single level of labels, there are significant advantages in using a second level of labels that are bound to IPv6 prefixes via MP-BGP advertisements. The use of a second level label allows Penultimate Hop Popping on the IPv4 label switching router upstream of the egress 6PE router without any IPv6 capability or upgrade on that router, because it still transmits MPLS packets even after the popping, instead of having to transmit IPv6 packets and encapsulate them appropriately. Also, an existing IPv4-signalled LSP that uses an IPv4 Explicit NULL label over the last hop could not be used to carry IPv6 with a single label, since the IPv4 Explicit NULL label cannot be used to carry native IPv6 traffic, while it could be used to carry labelled IPv6 traffic. This is why a second label MUST be used with the 6PE approach.

The label bound by MP-BGP to the IPv6 prefix indicates to the egress 6PE router that the packet is an IPv6 packet. That label MAY be an arbitrary value identifying an IPv6 routing context or outgoing interface to send the packet to, or MAY be the IPv6 Explicit Null Label, and an ingress 6PE router MUST be able to accept any such advertised label.
sections.plainLanguage: The ingress router imposes a label directly on the IPv6 header, without prepending an IPv4 header. A second label is still required. The outer label is the one for the IPv4-signalled path, and the inner label, bound to the IPv6 prefix by BGP, tells the egress router that the packet is IPv6 and which context to forward it in. The second label lets the penultimate router pop its label without needing IPv6 capability, and it lets an IPv4-signalled path that uses an IPv4 Explicit NULL label carry IPv6 traffic, which a single label could not do.

sections.title: The MTU Problem
sections.content:
IPv6 requires that every link in the IPv6 Internet have an MTU of 1280 octets or larger. Therefore, on MPLS links that are used for transport of IPv6 under the 6PE approach and that do not support link-specific fragmentation and reassembly, the MTU must be configured to at least 1280 octets plus the encapsulation overhead.

Some IPv6 hosts might send packets larger than the MTU available in the IPv4 MPLS core and rely on Path MTU discovery to learn about those links. To simplify MTU discovery operations, one option is for the network administrator to engineer the MTU on the core facing interfaces of the ingress 6PE consistent with the core MTU, so that ICMP 'Packet Too Big' messages can be sent back by the ingress 6PE without the corresponding packets ever entering the MPLS core. Otherwise, routers in the IPv4 MPLS network have the option to generate an ICMP 'Packet Too Big' message using the mechanisms described for tunnelling private addresses through a public backbone.

In that other case, should a core router with an outgoing link with an MTU smaller than 1280 receive an encapsulated IPv6 packet larger than 1280, the mechanisms of RFC 3032 may result in the 'Packet Too Big' message never reaching the sender. The core router builds the message filled with the invoking packet up to 1280 bytes, and when forwarding it downstream towards the egress provider edge, the MTU of the outgoing link causes the packet to be dropped. The originator of the packets will notice that its data is not getting through, without knowing why and where it is discarded. The RFC notes that this issue would only occur if the recommendation to configure the MTU on MPLS links of at least 1280 octets plus encapsulation overhead is not adhered to.
sections.plainLanguage: Every link in the IPv6 Internet must have an MTU of at least 1280 octets, so the MPLS links used to carry IPv6 must be configured to at least 1280 octets plus the encapsulation overhead, unless they support link-specific fragmentation. If that is not done, the ICMP 'Packet Too Big' message generated by a core router can be dropped on the way out, because it is filled with the invoking packet up to 1280 bytes, and the sender then sees its data disappear without knowing where. An alternative is to engineer the MTU on the core-facing interfaces of the ingress router to match the core, so the message never enters the core at all.

sections.title: Crossing Autonomous System Boundaries
sections.content:
When two IPv6 islands are connected to different Autonomous Systems, three main approaches are distinguished, mirroring the three approaches described for IPv4 VPNs.

Approach (a) is eBGP redistribution of IPv6 routes from AS to neighbouring AS. The 6PE routers use IBGP to redistribute labelled IPv6 routes either to an Autonomous System Border Router 6PE router, or to a route reflector of which such a router is a client. The border router then uses eBGP to redistribute the unlabelled IPv6 routes to a border router in another AS, which in turn distributes them to the 6PE routers in that AS. IPv6 needs to be activated on the inter-ASBR links, and each border router 6PE router has at least one IPv6 address on the interface to that link. No inter-AS LSPs are used: there is effectively a separate mesh of LSPs across the 6PE routers within each AS. The peering border router in the neighbouring AS redistributes these routes to the 6PEs in its AS using IBGP, encoding its own IPv4 address as the IPv4-mapped IPv6 BGP Next Hop.

Approach (b) is eBGP redistribution of labelled IPv6 routes. The border router uses eBGP to redistribute the labelled IPv6 routes to a border router in another AS, which distributes them to the 6PE routers in that AS. IPv6 may or may not be activated on the inter-ASBR links. This approach requires that there be label switched paths established across ASes, so the corresponding considerations for labelled IPv4 VPN routes apply equally. The border routers may peer over IPv4 or IPv6; when peering over IPv6, the exchange of labelled IPv6 routes follows the multiprotocol BGP and label binding rules, and when peering over IPv4 the exchange must encode the IPv4 address of the border router as an IPv4-mapped IPv6 address in the BGP Next Hop field.

Approach (c) is multi-hop eBGP redistribution of labelled IPv6 routes between source and destination ASes, with eBGP redistribution of labelled IPv4 routes from AS to neighbouring AS. IPv6 routes are neither maintained nor distributed by the border routers, and those routers need not be dual stack, but may be IPv4/MPLS-only routers. A border router maintains labelled IPv4 /32 routes to the 6PE routers within its AS and uses eBGP to distribute these routes to other ASes, which creates an IPv4 label switched path from the ingress 6PE to the egress 6PE. The 6PE routers in different ASes can then establish multi-hop eBGP connections to each other over IPv4 and exchange labelled IPv6 routes with an IPv4-mapped IPv6 next hop. IPv6 need not be activated on the inter-ASBR links, but IPv4 label switched paths must exist across the ASes leading from the ingress 6PE to the egress 6PE, and the exchange of IPv6 routes can only start after BGP has created IPv4 connectivity between the ASes.
sections.plainLanguage: When the two IPv6 islands are in different autonomous systems, three approaches are described. The border routers can exchange plain IPv6 routes with eBGP and redistribute them inside their own network, which needs no label-switched path across the border and needs IPv6 on the link between the border routers. Or they can exchange labelled IPv6 routes with eBGP, which needs labelled paths across the autonomous system boundaries and may leave IPv6 off the border link. Or the border routers can exchange only labelled IPv4 routes for the provider edge routers and let the 6PE routers in different autonomous systems peer with each other over multi-hop eBGP and exchange labelled IPv6 routes, which needs IPv4 paths across the boundaries but no IPv6 on them at all.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The extensions defined in this document allow BGP to propagate reachability information about IPv6 routes over an MPLS IPv4 core network. As such, no new security issues are raised beyond those that already exist in BGP-4 and use of MP-BGP for IPv6, and the security features of BGP and the corresponding security policy defined in the ISP domain are applicable. For the inter-AS distribution of IPv6 routes according to case (a), no new security issues are raised beyond those that already exist in the use of eBGP for IPv6.

For the inter-AS distribution of IPv6 routes according to cases (b) and (c), the procedures require that there be label switched paths established across the AS boundaries, so the appropriate trust relationships must exist between and among the set of ASes along the path. Care must be taken to avoid label spoofing. To this end an ASBR 6PE SHOULD only accept labelled packets from its peer ASBR 6PE if the topmost label is a label that it has explicitly signalled to that peer.

For case (c), label spoofing may be more difficult to prevent. The MPLS label distributed with the IPv6 routes via multi-hop eBGP is sent directly from the egress 6PE to ingress 6PEs in another AS, or through route reflectors, and this label is advertised transparently through the AS boundaries. When the egress 6PE that sent the labelled IPv6 routes receives a data packet that has this particular label on top of its stack, it may not be able to verify whether the label was pushed on the stack by an ingress 6PE that is allowed to do so, so one AS may be vulnerable to label spoofing in a different AS. The RFC notes that addressing this particular security issue is for further study.
sections.plainLanguage: The extensions let BGP carry IPv6 reachability over an IPv4 core, so they raise no new security issues beyond those of BGP-4 and Multiprotocol BGP for IPv6, and the BGP security policy of the provider applies. The approaches that need labelled paths across autonomous system boundaries do need trust between the autonomous systems along the path, and care must be taken to avoid label spoofing. A border router should only accept labelled packets from its peer if the topmost label is one it explicitly signalled to that peer. The third approach is harder to protect, because the label is advertised transparently across the borders and one autonomous system may be exposed to spoofing from another.
